mainEntity.name: How much is a home in Piedmont Pines?

acceptedAnswer.text: The typical home value in Piedmont Pines is $1,295,408 as of 2026-09-30, down 0.01 percent from the month before and up 3.2 percent over the year. That is the Zillow Home Value Index. It estimates the typical value of every home in the area, listed or not. The median asking price of what is actually on the market in Oakland is $674,250. Those two numbers measure different populations and they do not have to agree. For one specific house instead of the typical one, that is a comparable sales analysis, and it is a different exercise than reading an index.

mainEntity.name: What is the Piedmont Pines ZIP code?

acceptedAnswer.text: Against the rest of Oakland, yes. Piedmont Pines ranks 14 of 121 neighborhoods by typical value, and at $1,295,408 it sits 82 percent above the citywide typical value of $710,647. The monthly number is the one I would focus on: owning the typical home here runs about $12,282 a month once you include the loan, property tax, insurance, utilities and a maintenance budget. The full breakdown is in the cost of holding section above.

mainEntity.name: What are property taxes in Oakland?

acceptedAnswer.text: I use 1.71 percent in this report, the Oakland effective rate. On a home at $1,295,408 that is roughly $1,846 a month, $22,151 a year. Proposition 13 sets the base at 1 percent of assessed value and caps growth in that assessed value at 2 percent a year while one owner holds the property, and voter-approved bonds sit on top. The real rate runs above 1 percent. The part that catches buyers is that a purchase resets assessed value to the price paid. Any figure you read that was built from median taxes actually paid is averaging in decades of protected assessments and will understate what a new buyer owes.

mainEntity.name: What is the transfer tax in Oakland?

acceptedAnswer.text: This is the cost people forget to budget for, and it varies more by city line than anything else in a California transaction. Oakland is a chartered city, so the rate here is $16.10 per $1,000 of value. On a home at $1,295,408 that is $20,856. For scale, the identical sale price would carry $1,425 in Dublin and $20,856 in Oakland, both in this same county. There is also a cliff worth knowing about. The rate applies to the whole value, not just the portion above a threshold, so crossing $2,000,000 reprices the entire sale. At exactly $2,000,000 the tax is $32,200. One dollar higher it is $37,200. That is $5,000 for one dollar of price. The typical home here is $704,592 below that line. That makes it a live pricing question and not a theoretical one. Who pays is set by the contract and by local custom, not by statute, and it is negotiable. Escrow is the authority on the exact figure for a specific sale.

mainEntity.name: What is the FHA loan limit in Oakland?

acceptedAnswer.text: For 2026 the one-unit limit in Alameda County is $1,249,125, and that figure is both the conforming conventional ceiling and the FHA ceiling. Here is why that matters in Piedmont Pines. At the typical value of $1,295,408, a minimum-down loan would be $1,250,069. That is $944 over the ceiling. To get inside it you would need $46,283 down, about 4 percent. The most expensive home a 3.5 percent down FHA loan reaches in this county is around $1,294,430. This is the single most common thing I see people find out too late.

mainEntity.name: What first-time buyer help is available in Oakland?

acceptedAnswer.text: CalHFA runs the statewide programs and they layer on top of a first mortgage and do not replace it. MyHome is a deferred-payment junior loan toward the down payment and closing costs, open year round. ZIP covers closing costs on a CalHFA conventional first. Dream For All is the shared-appreciation program, limited to first-generation buyers, and it runs in announced windows, not continuously. GSFA Platinum is a separate option, and Oakland and Alameda County run their own programs on their own funding cycles. Those are the ones most people never hear about. The constraint that actually binds in a neighborhood at $1,295,408 is almost never income. It is the program's own purchase price cap, often set below the county loan limit. I would establish the price a program allows first, then shop inside it. Doing it the other way around is how people fall for a house the assistance cannot reach.

mainEntity.name: Can I build an ADU in Oakland?

acceptedAnswer.text: Almost certainly yes, in some form. State law requires local agencies to allow accessory dwelling units on residential lots with ministerial approval and a decision deadline, so the real question is what size and configuration the local ordinance permits, not whether you are allowed. Owner-occupancy requirements on new ADUs have been removed, so the main house and the ADU can both be rented. Selling one separately is a different question. Assembly Bill 1033 lets a city allow an ADU to be sold as its own condominium unit, but it is permissive and not mandatory, relatively few cities have adopted an enabling ordinance, and without one there is no right to do it. That is a question for the Oakland planning department and the municipal code, not something the state law answers on its own.

mainEntity.name: Is the Oakland housing market slowing down?

acceptedAnswer.text: I would rather give you the two numbers that disagree than a verdict. Typical home value in Piedmont Pines is down 0.01 percent month over month and up 3.2 percent year over year. Realtor.com does not publish listing comparisons for Oakland this month, so the value series above is the only trend figure I can stand behind here. More supply and a slower pace sitting alongside a higher typical value is a composition effect, not a contradiction. Anyone giving you a one-word answer about a market this specific is not looking at it closely.

mainEntity.name: How much is home insurance in Oakland?

acceptedAnswer.text: I use $215 a month, $2,580 a year, the California statewide average. A real quote on a specific house moves with the structure, the roof, the replacement cost and the wildfire risk rating on the parcel, so treat the average as a placeholder until you have a quote. One thing worth flagging: a vacant home is a different and more expensive class of policy. That catches sellers who move out before closing, and it catches estates almost every time.
